items.topic: What a quick knockout search cannot tell you
items.hook: Searching the exact spelling is the easiest part of clearance. It is also the least useful.
items.visual_concept: A fine mesh screen catching large particles while smaller ones pass through, macro, cool light
key_points: Exact-match searching only rules out the most obvious conflicts
Phonetic equivalents and visual near-matches carry the real risk
Related goods and services widen the field considerably
Pending applications matter even though they are not yet registered
items.caption_body:
Typing your name into a database and getting no exact match feels conclusive. It is the beginning of the work, not the end.

Conflicts rarely look identical. They sound alike. They share a dominant element. They mean the same thing in a different word. They sit in a class you did not think to check but that a buyer would see as related.

And pending applications, not yet registered, still shape what is available.

A clearance review is a search for the things that do not match on the surface. That is where applications actually fail.

items.hook: Two names that look different on paper can be the same name out loud.
items.visual_concept: Overlapping concentric sound-wave rings rendered as thin teal arcs on deep navy
key_points: Marks are compared by sound as well as by appearance
Consumers often encounter brands verbally — recommendations, radio, voice search
Deliberate respellings usually share the same pronunciation
Sound similarity alone can be enough to raise a conflict
items.caption_body:
Say your shortlist out loud. Then say the names already in your category.

Marks are compared on sound as well as sight, because that is how a great deal of brand discovery actually happens — a recommendation across a table, a mention on a podcast, a voice assistant taking an order.

Which is why a clever respelling rarely creates distance. If the two names are indistinguishable when spoken, the spelling difference is doing less work than you think.

Read the shortlist aloud. It is the simplest clearance test there is.

items.topic: Why conflicts appear in categories you did not file in
items.hook: Your competition for a name is wider than your competition for customers.
items.visual_concept: A cluster of matte tiles at varying heights, adjacent ones sharing a teal edge
key_points: Confusion analysis considers whether goods and services are related, not identical
Adjacent categories can conflict — apparel and accessories, software and consulting
Channels of trade and typical buyers are part of the assessment
A mark in a neighbouring class can still block you
items.caption_body:
People search their own class and conclude the coast is clear.

The analysis is not that narrow. It asks whether the goods or services are related closely enough that a buyer might assume a common source. Apparel and accessories. Software and the consulting built around it. Beverages and the bar that serves them.

It also looks at how the products reach people and who buys them.

So a registration sitting in a class you never considered can still stand in your way — because to a customer, the two businesses would look connected.

items.topic: Looking for businesses that never registered anything
items.hook: The riskiest conflicts are often the ones that never filed.
items.visual_concept: Faint structures emerging from deep shadow under a single low raking light
key_points: Common-law users can hold rights without any registration
They will not appear on the federal register
Trade directories, marketplaces and local listings are part of a thorough review
An unregistered prior user can still challenge your use
items.caption_body:
A register search shows you who filed. It does not show you who has simply been trading.

Businesses build common-law rights by using a mark in commerce, with no paperwork at all. They are invisible on the federal register and entirely real in a dispute.

Which is why a proper clearance review looks past the register — at marketplaces, directories, social handles, local listings, industry press. The places a business exists before it ever thinks about filing.

The conflict that surprises people is almost never the registered one. It is the one that was there all along.

items.topic: The right moment to run a clearance search
items.hook: Search when the name is still a candidate, not when it is already on the sign.
items.visual_concept: A branching path abstracted into thin luminous rails, one branch still open
key_points: Clearance is easiest while you still have alternatives
Once packaging, signage and accounts exist, changing costs far more
Search before committing spend, not after
Shortlisting several names makes a clean result more likely
items.caption_body:
The value of a clearance search is highest at the exact moment it feels least urgent — when the name is still one of several.

At that point, a problem is information. You cross a name off and move to the next.

Run the same search after the packaging is printed, the signage is up and two years of customers know the name, and the identical result becomes a crisis with a budget attached.

Nothing about the search changed. What changed is the weight a bad answer now carries.

Shortlist three. Clear them. Then commit.

items.topic: How to read a search result that is not a clean yes
items.hook: Most clearance results are not yes or no. They are how much risk.
items.visual_concept: A gradient scale rendered as stacked matte bars ascending left to right
key_points: Very few names come back with zero related marks
The question is how close, how related, and how strong the other mark is
Some risks can be managed by narrowing the description
Understanding the risk is what lets you make an informed decision
items.caption_body:
People expect a clearance search to return a verdict. It usually returns a picture.

Almost every name has something in its neighbourhood. What matters is how close that something is, how related the goods are, how strong the other mark is, and whether the owner has a history of defending it.

Some risks are worth accepting. Some can be reduced by narrowing how you describe your goods and services. Some are clear signals to pick a different name.

The point of the search is not a stamp. It is knowing which of those three you are looking at before you spend anything.

items.topic: Clearing several names at once instead of one
items.hook: Fall in love with one name and you have no leverage.
items.visual_concept: Three parallel matte columns of unequal height, one lit in teal
key_points: A single favourite makes a bad result feel like a disaster
Clearing a shortlist keeps the decision commercial rather than emotional
Alternatives cost far less to consider before launch
The strongest names are often not the first choice
items.caption_body:
The most expensive thing in naming is not a bad name. It is a favourite.

Once a founder has settled on one word, every clearance result becomes a negotiation with reality. People start reasoning around risks they would never accept if the name were still one of three.

So carry a shortlist into clearance. Three names you would genuinely be happy with. Let the search tell you which one is cleanest.

You end up with a stronger mark and a decision you are not arguing yourself into.

items.topic: What you can check yourself before asking for help
items.hook: You can do the first hour of clearance yourself. Here is what it covers.
items.visual_concept: A workbench surface in cool grey with a single precision tool, shallow depth of field
key_points: Public trademark search tools are free and worth using early
Marketplace, social and directory searches surface unregistered users
Saying the name aloud catches phonetic near-matches
A self-check narrows the shortlist; it does not replace a full review
items.caption_body:
You do not need anyone to run the first pass. Do this before you get attached.

Search the public trademark database for the exact word and for the obvious variants. Search the marketplaces where your category sells. Search social handles. Search the name plus your industry.

Then say it out loud and search what it sounds like, not what it looks like.

That hour will remove the worst candidates from your shortlist for free.

What it will not do is tell you how a near-match in a related class would actually be assessed. That is the part worth handing over.
